headline: High: shared filesystem and writable outputs create prompt-injection, leakage, and edit-conflict risks; Mentat’s broad egress raises cascading-error and compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A writes and reads files in shared skill paths, while agent B’s state is shared via filesystem and it reads/writes selected files. That creates a plausible file-based injection bridge even without MCP or clipboard. The pair is not documented as directly integrated, so I avoid high, but the shared workspace makes instruction hijacking realistic.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory tree, file content can be treated as instructions by B.
IF A writes attacker-controlled text into shared skill files, B may ingest it on later runs.
mitigations: Separate working directories per agent.
Mark shared files read-only for B.
Add a manual review step before B consumes A-authored files.
Use filename allowlists for any cross-agent handoff.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches marketing and product-marketing context, and B reads/writes source files while sending content to a configured model provider. If they share a workspace, A’s content can flow into B’s prompts and then to a third-party API. This is not proven by direct integration, but the filesystem bridge and B’s outbound model calls make leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF A and B share files containing marketing or product context, B can upload that content to its model provider.
IF B is pointed at files authored by A, those contents may leave the local environment via API calls.
mitigations: Keep sensitive marketing files out of B’s input set.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Disable B on directories containing confidential drafts.
Review outbound prompts before model calls.
requires-engineering: enforce data-class filtering at the orchestrator.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, and B can modify git state while A can spawn subprocesses and also write files. B’s shared-state model is explicitly via filesystem, so concurrent edits to the same repo or workspace can race and overwrite each other. Because git state corruption can be irreversible and the overlap is in default capabilities, this is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository, concurrent writes can clobber each other.
IF B modifies git state while A writes files in the same tree, history or working tree can diverge.
mitigations: Run agents in separate clones.
Serialize access with a lock file.
Require one agent to be read-only.
Commit after each agent’s turn.
requires-engineering: add workspace-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces marketing content and product-marketing context, and B is a coding assistant that can turn file contents into diffs and model-provider calls. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, a mistaken marketing claim can propagate into code, docs, or commits. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as source material without verification, errors can be propagated into edits or commits.
IF A’s marketing claims are copied into B’s outputs, downstream artifacts may inherit those claims.
mitigations: Require source verification before B edits.
Have a human approve A-generated claims.
Keep A’s outputs out of B’s default context.
Add a checklist for factual claims.
requires-engineering: add citation/verification gating.

E_compliance.rationale: A is a marketing agent touching marketing context, while B handles source code and model-provider API keys. No explicit residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented, so I do not escalate to medium. However, B’s broad egress and API-key handling create a small compliance gap if marketing materials contain restricted data and are routed through B.
conditions: IF restricted marketing data is placed into B’s prompts, it may be transmitted to a third-party model provider.
IF retention rules differ between A-authored files and B’s logs, compliance handling can diverge.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from B inputs.
Review retention settings for model-provider logs.
Use a DPA-approved provider configuration.
Document which data classes may cross the boundary.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class.
